covers.quote: Use initial capitals for commercial terms
An exception to using initial capitals is where the business itself uses an unusual mix of spacing, capitals and lower case letters. In this case, write it the way the business writes it.

examples.note: Initial capitals for trade marks.
Exceptions where unusual spacing or capitals are used by the business.
Contrast pairs showing capitalisation when used as a trade mark versus lower case when used generically.

rules.quote: Use initial capitals for trade marks, brands and business names.
rules.violation_condition: a trade mark, brand, or business name written without initial capitals
when: unless the business itself uses an unusual mix of spacing, capitals and lower case letters
rules.why: G-1: The heading 'Use initial capitals for commercial terms' groups its children and is absorbed into the specific rule. G-2: Exceptions for unusual capitalisation are recorded under 'when'.

rules.quote: Don’t use an initial capital at the start of sentences when the trade mark or brand starts with a lower case letter.
rules.violation_condition: an initial capital at the start of a sentence for a trade mark or brand that officially starts with a lower case letter
rules.why: Specific rule concerning the start of sentences for unusually-capitalised brands.

rules.quote: Use initial capitals for the proprietary names of drugs and other chemicals, but lower case for generic names.
rules.violation_condition: a proprietary drug or chemical name written without initial capitals, or a generic drug or chemical name written with initial capitals

covers.quote: You should also spell ‘trade mark’ as 2 words when you use it as a verb, although it’s better to say ‘register a trade mark’.

examples.note: Used as a noun.

parts.quote: The trade mark Vegemite was first registered in 1923.

examples.note: Used as a verb.

parts.quote: Trade mark your brand if you don’t want other organisations or businesses to use it.
Register your brand as a trade mark if you don’t want others to use it.

rules.quote: ‘Trade mark’ is spelled as 2 words in the Trade Marks Act 1995. Use this spelling when writing for government, even though most dictionaries prefer ‘trademark’.
rules.violation_condition: the word 'trademark' spelled as a single word
rules.why: Consolidates the spelling requirement for 'trade mark' across noun and verb usages.

covers.quote: Use a common word for a product if you can

examples.note: Generic alternatives.
Trade marks to avoid.

rules.quote: Avoid using trade marks and brand names if possible. Instead use a generic word.
rules.specification: Do not use a trade mark or brand name; use its generic equivalent.
rules.violation_condition: a trade mark or brand name used when a generic word is available
rules.why: G-1: Heading groups the rule and is covered. G-4: Rule restated from heading.

rules.quote: Avoid using the registered (®) symbol or the trade mark (™) symbol for trade marks if possible.
rules.violation_condition: the registered symbol (®) or the trade mark symbol (™) used next to a trade mark

rules.quote: If a term is still registered as a trade mark, you should use it only for that brand and use a capital letter.
rules.violation_condition: a registered trade mark used to refer to a product of a different brand or a generic product
rules.why: Distinct rule regarding the legal usage of a trade mark compared to generic usage.

examples.note: Genericized names starting with lower case.

rules.quote: Other brand names have become so widely used that they are no longer associated with a specific product. They have become common household names used in a generic sense. They start with lower case except at the start of a sentence.
rules.specification: Start genericized trademarks with a lower case letter.
rules.violation_condition: a genericized former brand name written with an initial capital letter when not at the start of a sentence
when: unless at the start of a sentence
rules.why: Exception/distinct rule for former trademarks that have become fully genericized.
